 Cyber outages live updates: Gmail, Apple Pay, iCloud the latest to go down — but FEMA test goes off without a hitch 
 By 
 Kaydi Pelletier 
 Updated 
 Nov. 17, 2026, 2:25 p.m. ET 
 See more of our coverage in your search results. 
 Make New York Post a Preferred Source 
 Gmail, Apple Pay, iCloud and more major online services Americans rely on daily are experiencing outages Tuesday — after Chase bank, United Airlines, Microsoft and more companies saw widespread outages that began last week. 
 A highly classified National Security Agency communications network also went offline Tuesday, according to reports.
 On top of that, the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) was set to test its Emergency Alert System at 2:20 p.m. ET on Tuesday. 
 Though some people on the internet had been spiraling over unfounded conspiracy theories that the test would prompt a 90-day nationwide blackout, the regularly scheduled maintenance check went off without a hitch.
 Follow live updates for the latest news on outages and reactions to FEMA’s emergency alert test: 
 8 minutes ago FEMA sends emergency alert test amid reported Gmail, Apple, bank outages
 By 
 Kaydi Pelletier It's 2:25 — are your lights still on?
 The Federal Emergency Management Agency sent a test of its Emergency Alert System right on time Tuesday, at 2:20 p.m. ET, in coordination with the FCC.
 I can report that here in the heart of midtown Manhattan, the lights are in fact still on, despite unsubstantiated claims that the test — which FEMA must carry out every three years to comply with federal law — would trigger a 90-day nationwide blackout.
 So far, so good.
 15 minutes ago Why is FEMA testing the Emergency Alert System today?
 By 
 Kaydi Pelletier FEMA is about to test its Emergency Alert System. But why?
 The short answer: because it's required by federal law.
 FEMA must test the system at least once every three years to make ensure the system is effective before it's needed in an actual emergency.
 It last tested the EAS in 2023, so the 2:20 p.m. ET test comes right on schedule.
 34 minutes ago Officials slap down conspiracy theories that test will trigger 90-day nationwide blackout 
 By 
 Kaydi Pelletier For more than a week, people have been spinning themselves (and others) into a tizzy on social media about FEMA and the FCC's joint scheduled test of the Emergency Alert System .
 As it does, the Internet was gonna Internet — and somehow theories began flying that the EAS test would prompt a 90-day blackout across the US Tuesday afternoon when it goes out.
 However, officials say the unfounded fears are just that: unfounded, and not going to happen.
 It's unclear where the theories about an imminent 90-day blackout originated. but on Monday, FEMA said , essentially, "nothing to see here":
 We’ve heard a lot of rumors about tomorrow’s EAS test. 📺📻 Let’s clear things up. It lasts 1 minute, and no action is required. No blackouts, no secret emergencies. Just our legally mandated, routine test on TV and radio at approximately 2:20 PM ET: https://t.co/WGD7xCuRDB pic.twitter.com/HEErLQVKga 
— FEMA (@fema) November 16, 2026 
 59 minutes ago Chaos across the web one hour before FEMA, FCC's Emergency Alert System test
 By 
 Kaydi Pelletier The Federal Emergency Management Agency and the Federal Communications Commission are set to conduct a joint, nationwide test of the Emergency Alert System across TV and radio at 2:20 p.m. ET Tuesday.
 The planned test had social media users spiraling with unfounded theories that the test will trigger a 90-day power blackout across the country — even before the epic, two-day Microsoft outage last week, and the rare nationwide FAA ground stop of all flights that followed on Friday.
 1 hour ago Charles Schwab says 'brief webpage loading issue' is fixed
 By 
 Kaydi Pelletier People began reporting problems with Charles Schwab's website around 10 a.m. ET Tuesday, with the outage reports spiking shortly after.
 However, just after 12 p.m., the "brief webpage loading issue" had been resolved, the company said on X .
 A brief webpage loading issue has been resolved. Trading remained available, and clients could access their accounts at https://t.co/GmzwrfGKkd or through the Schwab Mobile app. We apologize for the inconvenience.
— Charles Schwab Corp (@CharlesSchwab) November 17, 2026
